beats.text: Video world models usually choke on long-horizon generation because their memory usage grows linearly, eventually crashing your VRAM with redundant, bloated latent feature tensors.
beats.visual_focus: A bar chart showing memory usage exploding as frames increase, with a red warning light flashing.

beats.text: Imagine trying to store every page of a book in a single folder; eventually, the folder bursts. That is how standard video models handle scene history.
beats.visual_focus: An animation of a folder expanding until it physically tears apart under the weight of too many paper sheets.

beats.text: Enter Honeycomb. It uses HexMemory, a low-rank representation that compresses the entire 3D scene into exactly six fixed spatial and spatiotemporal planes.
beats.visual_focus: A 3D cube unfolding into six flat planes, representing the HexMemory architecture.

beats.text: The writer warps existing planes to match new chunks, then fuses them with a learned residual correction, keeping the total memory footprint perfectly constant.

feynman_certification.listener_verdict: The hook was solid—I've definitely hit that VRAM wall before, so I stayed. I liked that you didn't treat me like a toddler with 'smart folders.' However, when you hit Beat 4, you lost me a bit. I get the 'constant memory' goal, but 'learned residual correction' sounds like a black box. I'd love to know if that's just a small MLP or a specific attention layer doing the heavy lifting.
